faqs.question: Does this mean stolen credentials are no longer a major risk?
faqs.answer: No — credential-based attacks remain extremely common. What changed is the ranking: vulnerability exploitation moved into first place for the first time in the report's 19-year history, meaning it now narrowly leads, not that credential theft has become rare.

faqs.question: If we already run vulnerability scans, are we covered?
faqs.answer: Scanning identifies that a vulnerability exists. It does not close the gap between disclosure and exploitation, which is the actual problem driving this shift. Scanning plus a slow patching process is functionally similar to not scanning at all, from an attacker's perspective, if the window between the two is still measured in weeks.

faqs.question: What is an "N-day" vulnerability, and why does it matter more than zero-days here?
faqs.answer: An N-day vulnerability is one that is already publicly known and has a patch available — "N" days after disclosure, as opposed to a zero-day, which has no patch yet. Most real-world exploitation targets N-days, not zero-days, because organizations are slow to patch even known, fixable issues. That gap, not undiscovered flaws, is where most of this risk actually lives.

title: AI Security Risks Every Business Should Understand
description: Adopting AI tools introduces a specific set of security risks — prompt injection, data leakage, and unsanctioned "shadow AI" use — distinct from traditional software risk. Here is what actually matters.
bodyMarkdown:
Adopting AI tools — whether a customer support assistant, an internal automation, or an AI coding assistant — introduces a set of security risks that are genuinely different from traditional software risk, not just a new flavour of the same old problems. Understanding the specific, current shape of that risk is more useful than either blanket AI enthusiasm or blanket AI avoidance.

## The reference points: NIST and OWASP

Two authoritative sources define the current shape of AI security risk. **NIST's AI Risk Management Framework**, and specifically its **Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1)**, explicitly identifies direct and indirect prompt injection and data poisoning as information security risks, and flags supply chain integrity — the trustworthiness of the models and components an application is built on — as a related value-chain risk. NIST's broader AI 100-2 taxonomy classifies attacks against AI systems into four categories: evasion, poisoning, privacy, and misuse.

On the application security side, **OWASP's Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications** now lists **prompt injection as LLM01** — the single most significant risk category — and the 2025 edition added new categories including **System Prompt Leakage** and **Vector and Embedding Weaknesses**, reflecting how retrieval-augmented and increasingly autonomous ("agentic") AI systems have expanded what there is to attack.

## The three risks that matter most for a business, not just a developer

**Prompt injection.** An AI system that reads external content — a customer's uploaded document, a webpage it's summarising, an incoming email it's triaging — can be manipulated if that content contains hidden instructions designed to redirect the AI's behaviour. This matters commercially wherever an AI tool acts on external input with any degree of autonomy: an AI assistant that can send emails, update records, or trigger a workflow based on what it reads is a meaningfully different risk than one that only displays a summary for a human to review.

**Data leakage through AI tools.** Many AI tools, particularly consumer-facing ones, don't offer strong guarantees about how submitted data is stored, retained, or used — including, in some cases, for further model training. An employee pasting client contract details, source code, or financial data into an AI tool to "save time" can inadvertently expose that data outside the business's control, with no way to retract it afterward.

**Shadow AI.** This is the adoption pattern that makes the first two risks harder to manage: employees adopting AI tools the business hasn't reviewed, approved, or configured, simply because the tool is useful and easy to access. The risk isn't necessarily the tool itself — it's the complete lack of visibility into what data has gone where, which makes even asking "have we been exposed?" difficult to answer after the fact.

## Why this connects directly to how AI automation should be built

None of this is an argument against using AI. It's an argument for building AI automation with the same security discipline applied to any other system handling business data — arguably more, given how new and fast-moving the risk landscape is. Concretely, that means designing for data minimisation (each step of an automation only sees the data it actually needs), human review on high-stakes actions rather than full autonomy by default, and clear documentation of exactly which third-party AI services are involved and what happens to data sent to them.

## Security recommendations

- **Establish an approved-tools policy for AI use**, and make the approved option genuinely convenient — shadow AI usually happens because the sanctioned alternative is slower or missing entirely, not out of malice.
- **Treat AI-generated actions with consequences (sending communications, modifying records, approving transactions) as requiring human review**, at least until an automation has a strong track record and a low-consequence failure mode.
- **Validate content before an AI system acts on it**, the same way you'd validate any external input — this is the direct defence against prompt injection.
- **Document data flows for every AI tool in use**, including what's sent to third-party model providers and under what terms, so you can actually answer "where does our data go" when asked.
- **Review AI tool contracts for data retention and training-use terms** before adopting them for anything involving client or sensitive business data.

## Key takeaways

AI security risk in 2026 has a specific, documented shape — prompt injection, data leakage, and unsanctioned shadow AI use — rather than being a vague, generic "AI is risky" concern. NIST and OWASP both treat these as concrete, addressable risks with known mitigations, not unsolvable problems. The businesses getting real value from AI safely are the ones designing automation with data minimisation and human review built in from the start, not adding security as an afterthought.

faqs.answer: Prompt injection is when an attacker hides instructions inside content an AI system will process — a document, a webpage, an email — hoping the AI follows those hidden instructions instead of (or in addition to) the task its owner actually intended. OWASP ranks it as the top security risk for large language model applications.

faqs.answer: Shadow AI refers to employees using AI tools the business has not approved, reviewed, or configured securely — often to save time on a task. The risk is not the AI tool itself, but that sensitive company or client data may be pasted into a public tool with no visibility into how that data is stored, used, or retained.

faqs.answer: Yes. NIST published the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST-AI-600-1), which explicitly identifies prompt injection and data poisoning as information security risks, and supply chain integrity as a related concern for organisations building on third-party AI models.

title: API Security in 2026: OWASP API Top 10 and the Rise of Agentic Risk
description: APIs are now called by AI agents as often as by people. Here is what the OWASP API Security Top 10 covers, why it still matters, and what changes when software calls your API instead of a human.
bodyMarkdown:
APIs used to be called mostly by other pieces of software written by people who understood the API's intended use. That's changing. Agentic AI systems — tools that autonomously discover endpoints, chain multiple API calls together, and make decisions about what to call next — are now a growing share of real API traffic. Service-mesh measurements already show that 60–80% of API calls inside typical microservices environments are service-to-service rather than human-initiated. The risk model behind API security hasn't been thrown out because of this, but it has shifted in ways worth understanding.

## The OWASP API Security Top 10 is still the reference point

Unlike the main OWASP Top 10, which OWASP just refreshed for 2025, the [OWASP API Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/API-Security/) hasn't had a 2026 update — the current, authoritative version is still the 2023 edition. That doesn't mean it's outdated; the underlying weakness patterns it describes are structural, not tied to a particular year's threat headlines:

- **API1: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA).** The most common and most damaging API weakness. An endpoint checks that you're logged in, but not that the specific record you're requesting belongs to you.
- **API2: Broken Authentication.** Weak, guessable, or improperly validated tokens and credentials.
- **API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization.** Similar to BOLA, but at the field level — you can view or edit specific fields (like a salary or an admin flag) you shouldn't be able to touch.
- **API4: Unrestricted Resource Consumption.** No limits on how many requests, how much data, or how expensive a query a single caller can make — opening the door to both abuse and denial-of-service.
- **API5: Broken Function Level Authorization.** A regular user can call an endpoint intended only for administrators, because the API doesn't check role, only login status.
- **API6: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows.** An API technically works as designed, but nothing stops it being automated at a scale that damages the business — for example, buying out limited inventory via a purchase endpoint.
- **API7: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).** The API can be tricked into making requests to internal systems on the caller's behalf.
- **API8: Security Misconfiguration.** Default settings, verbose error messages, missing security headers — the same class of issue that jumped to #2 in the 2025 main OWASP Top 10.
- **API9: Improper Inventory Management.** Old, forgotten, or undocumented API versions still running and still reachable.
- **API10: Unsafe Consumption of APIs.** Trusting data or responses from third-party APIs without validating them, the same way you'd validate user input.

## What actually changes with agentic AI callers

The list above doesn't need to change to remain relevant, but the _consequences_ of getting it wrong shift when the caller is an autonomous agent rather than a person clicking through a UI:

- **Speed and scale of exploitation increase.** A person probing for a BOLA vulnerability tests a handful of IDs manually. An agentic system can enumerate thousands of IDs in the time it takes a human to notice the traffic spike.
- **Business logic abuse (API6) becomes easier to automate at scale.** An agent designed to "complete a task efficiently" has no inherent sense that hammering a checkout endpoint 10,000 times is abusive rather than efficient.
- **Improper inventory management (API9) matters more.** Agentic systems are often given broad discovery capability — they're built to find and use whatever APIs are reachable. A forgotten, undocumented internal endpoint that was low-risk when only a handful of engineers knew it existed becomes a live target the moment something is actively scanning for reachable endpoints.
- **Unsafe consumption of third-party APIs (API10) compounds with AI supply chains.** If your application calls an AI model API, and that API's output is trusted without validation, you've effectively extended your trust boundary to a system you don't control.

Security teams surveyed on this are already uneasy: a large majority report being very concerned about AI-enhanced attacks on their APIs, and a significant share admit they aren't confident their current security investment addresses it.

## Security recommendations

- **Enforce object-level authorization on every endpoint that accepts an ID**, not just the ones handling obviously sensitive data. Assume every ID-based lookup needs an ownership check.
- **Apply rate limiting and resource quotas per caller**, not just per API key tier, so a single automated client can't exhaust capacity or abuse a business flow.
- **Maintain a real, current API inventory.** If you don't know an endpoint exists, you can't secure it, and an increasing share of attackers — human or automated — actively hunt for exactly this gap.
- **Validate responses from third-party and AI-model APIs** the same way you'd validate user-submitted input, especially before that data influences a decision or gets rendered elsewhere.
- **Test authorization logic specifically during a penetration test**, separate from authentication. A test that confirms "login works" hasn't touched most of the OWASP API Top 10.

## Key takeaways

The OWASP API Security Top 10 hasn't changed in 2026, and it doesn't need to — object-level and function-level authorization failures remain the core, structural risk. What has changed is who's calling your APIs: an increasing share of traffic comes from autonomous agents that can find and abuse a weakness far faster than a human tester or attacker could. The fix isn't a different checklist; it's applying the existing one with the assumption that whatever can be called, will be called, repeatedly and at machine speed.

faqs.question: Is there a 2026 version of the OWASP API Security Top 10?
faqs.answer: No. As of late 2026, the current, authoritative version remains the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023 edition). There is no 2026 update to that specific list, though the surrounding threat landscape — particularly AI agents calling APIs — has shifted materially since 2023.

faqs.question: What is Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), and why is it always at the top of these lists?
faqs.answer: BOLA happens when an API lets a user access or modify an object — an order, an account, a file — that belongs to someone else, simply by changing an ID in the request. It tops API security lists because it is common (it is an easy mistake to make at scale) and severe (it directly exposes other users' data) at the same time.

faqs.question: Does having API authentication (API keys, OAuth) mean our APIs are secure?
faqs.answer: Authentication confirms who is calling your API. It does not confirm what that caller is allowed to do once authenticated. Most of the OWASP API Top 10 — including BOLA, broken function-level authorization, and excessive data exposure — are authorization problems that exist even with strong authentication in place.

title: Business Email Compromise in 2026: How Attackers Bypass MFA
description: Multi-factor authentication stops most credential attacks, but not all of them. Here is how modern business email compromise campaigns get around MFA, based on 2026 threat data from Microsoft.
bodyMarkdown:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is, correctly, the standard advice for stopping credential-based attacks — and it works, for most of them. But "most" isn't "all," and the gap between those two words is exactly where a growing share of business email compromise (BEC) activity now lives. Understanding how attackers get around MFA — rather than assuming it's an unbeatable wall — is what actually keeps a business protected.

## The scale, per Microsoft's own 2026 data

Microsoft's threat intelligence team publishes a quarterly email threat landscape report, and the 2026 numbers are large by any measure. In Q1 2026, Microsoft detected approximately **8.3 billion phishing emails**. That volume dropped somewhat to **7.6 billion in Q2 2026**, coinciding with Microsoft's disruption of a major phishing-as-a-service platform known as Tycoon2FA — a takedown that produced a measurable 15% decrease in phishing volume and forced attackers to shift tactics.

Business email compromise specifically accounted for roughly **10.7 million attacks in Q1 2026** alone. Interestingly, the content of most of these wasn't the obvious "urgent wire transfer" scam you might picture — Microsoft's data shows **82–84% of BEC content was generic outreach**, with explicit financial or document requests making up only 9–10%. In other words, most attacks start as a plausible, low-pressure message intended to start a conversation and build trust, with the actual ask coming later, once the target has already engaged.

## How MFA actually gets bypassed

MFA remains genuinely effective against the most common attack pattern: an attacker who has stolen a password (through a data breach, reuse, or a basic phishing page) and tries to log in with it. Without the second factor, that login fails. The bypass techniques that matter operate differently:

- **Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing**, the technique behind platforms like Tycoon2FA, works by proxying the _real_ login session in real time. The victim lands on a page that looks identical to their actual login screen, enters their password, and completes their real MFA prompt — but the attacker's server sits between the victim and the real service, capturing the resulting authenticated session token. From the service's point of view, this looks like a normal, successful, MFA-verified login, because in a technical sense, it was — just relayed through an attacker.
- **MFA fatigue** relies on repeatedly sending push notification approval requests until a tired or distracted user approves one just to make it stop, without checking whether they actually initiated the login.
- **Social engineering the reset process**, rather than attacking the login itself — convincing a help desk or the user to reset MFA entirely by impersonating IT support or the account owner.

None of these are "MFA doesn't work." They're evidence that MFA shifts the attack from stealing a password to hijacking a session or manipulating a person, which is a real improvement — but not the end of the story.

## The shift beyond email itself

Microsoft's Q2 2026 data also flags a tactical shift worth knowing about specifically because it's newer and less anticipated: as organisations get better at filtering email-based phishing, attackers have expanded into **Microsoft Teams-based social engineering**, including a reported roughly **tenfold increase in voice-based ("vishing") attempts** conducted through Teams calls. The logic is straightforward — email gets filtered and flagged more aggressively than it used to, so attackers move to channels with less mature filtering and a higher baseline of trust (an internal chat platform feels safer to employees than an unsolicited email, even when it shouldn't).

## Security recommendations

- **Use phishing-resistant MFA where possible** — hardware security keys or platform authenticators (like passkeys) that are cryptographically bound to the legitimate site, rather than a code or push approval that can be relayed through a proxy.
- **Train staff to verify unusual requests through a second channel**, especially anything involving payment, credential changes, or urgent action — a quick phone call to a known number catches almost everything AiTM phishing is designed to slip past.
- **Extend phishing awareness to Teams and other internal chat tools**, not just email. If your training only ever mentions "suspicious emails," you've left the fastest-growing channel uncovered.
- **Tighten help desk identity verification for MFA resets.** A process that resets MFA based on a phone call and a name is a bypass waiting to be used.
- **Monitor for impossible or unusual sign-in patterns** — a session originating from an unexpected location or device shortly after a legitimate-looking login is a strong signal, even when MFA was technically satisfied.

## Key takeaways

Business email compromise in 2026 isn't primarily about attackers cracking passwords — it's about patiently building trust through generic outreach, then either relaying a real login session past MFA or moving the conversation to a less-scrutinised channel like Teams. MFA remains essential and blocks the majority of attempts, but treating it as a complete solution — rather than one strong layer among several — is exactly the gap current attackers are trained to find.

faqs.answer: MFA blocks the large majority of automated, credential-stuffing style attacks, which is why it remains essential. It does not fully stop targeted phishing that uses a real-time proxy to capture both your password and your MFA approval at the same time, which is why MFA needs to be paired with user awareness and phishing-resistant methods where possible.

faqs.answer: Recent data shows most BEC content is generic outreach rather than an obviously fake invoice — a short, plausible message from what looks like a colleague or partner, designed to start a conversation before the request for money or data ever appears. That patience is what makes it hard to spot with a simple rule.

faqs.answer: Yes. Microsoft has reported a sharp rise in social engineering conducted over Microsoft Teams rather than email, including voice-based ("vishing") attempts, as attackers adapt to organisations that have gotten better at spotting email-based phishing.

title: Why Cloud Misconfiguration Is Now the Leading Cause of Data Breaches
description: Cloud breaches are rarely caused by the provider. Recent data shows misconfiguration — not a platform flaw — behind a growing share of incidents. Here is what that means and how to fix it.
bodyMarkdown:
When a cloud-hosted business gets breached, the instinct is often to ask whether AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud had a security failure. In the overwhelming majority of cases, they didn't. The infrastructure held. What failed was how the business configured what it built on top of that infrastructure — and current data shows this is now the dominant cause of cloud-related breaches, not an edge case.

## What the data actually shows

According to Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, cloud misconfiguration was responsible for 14% of all global breaches — up from 9% in 2024. That's a meaningful jump in a short window, and it tracks with how fast businesses have moved workloads to the cloud without a matching increase in configuration discipline.

Other figures paint a similar picture from different angles: over 31% of cloud breaches are attributed to misconfiguration and manual error, and a majority of organisations — around 70% — identify misconfigured cloud services as a major risk in their own environment. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach research puts a number on the damage: the average breach caused specifically by cloud misconfiguration costs **$4.45 million**.

Perhaps the most telling figure comes from Gartner, which has projected that through 2026, **99% of cloud security failures will be the customer's fault — not the provider's**. That's not a criticism of any particular business; it's a structural observation about how cloud security actually works.

## Why this keeps happening: the shared responsibility model

Every major cloud provider operates on a shared responsibility model. The provider secures the cloud itself — physical security, the hypervisor layer, network infrastructure, and the availability of the platform. The customer is responsible for security _in_ the cloud: how you configure identity and access management, how you set storage visibility, how you encrypt data, and how you segment your network.

The problem is that this split isn't always intuitive, especially for teams without a dedicated cloud security function. A storage bucket created during a quick prototype, left with default (often overly permissive) visibility settings, and never revisited once the project went to production, is a textbook example. It's not a sophisticated attack — it's a default that nobody changed.

## The three misconfiguration patterns that show up most often

- **Overly permissive identity and access management (IAM).** Users, service accounts, or applications granted far broader permissions than their actual job requires — often because it was faster to grant broad access during setup than to scope it precisely, with no follow-up to tighten it later.
- **Publicly exposed storage.** Object storage (the cloud equivalent of a shared drive) left visible to anyone with the link, or in some cases, anyone at all, when it was only ever meant to be accessed internally.
- **Missing or incomplete logging.** Weak identity controls or missing audit logging were found in a large majority of reviewed cloud accounts — meaning that even when something goes wrong, many organisations lack the visibility to know it happened, let alone respond quickly.

At scale, this adds up fast: research from cloud security vendors has found the average enterprise running **over 3,000 misconfigured cloud assets** at any given time. Most businesses don't have anywhere near that scale, but the same root causes — defaults never revisited, permissions never scoped down, logging never turned on — apply just as easily to a five-server environment as a five-thousand-server one.

## Security recommendations

- **Review IAM permissions against actual usage**, not against what seemed convenient at setup. Most cloud platforms provide tooling to show which granted permissions have actually been used — unused permissions are candidates for removal.
- **Audit storage visibility settings directly**, rather than assuming defaults are safe. Cloud storage defaults have improved over the years, but legacy resources created under older defaults are a common blind spot.
- **Turn on and actually monitor audit logging.** Logging that exists but nobody reviews provides no real protection — pair it with alerting on the events that matter (permission changes, new public access grants, unusual data access volume).
- **Treat cloud configuration review as ongoing, not one-time.** Environments drift as teams add resources, and a configuration that was correct at launch can quietly become permissive months later.
- **Get an independent review before, not after, an incident.** A cloud configuration review is far cheaper than the average $4.45 million cost of a breach it could have prevented.

## Key takeaways

The pattern in the current data is consistent across multiple independent sources: cloud breaches are overwhelmingly a configuration problem, not a provider problem. That's a genuinely useful thing to know, because unlike a zero-day vulnerability in provider infrastructure — which you can't do much about directly — misconfiguration is entirely within your control to find and fix, if someone actually looks.

Shahid Security's [Network & Cloud Security](/services/network-cloud-security/) service reviews AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud configurations against known-secure baselines, covering the exact patterns — IAM, storage visibility, logging — behind most reported cloud breaches.

**Not sure what your current cloud configuration actually exposes?** [Book a free consultation](/book/) and we'll help you find out before an attacker does.

faqs.answer: Cloud providers secure the infrastructure — physical data centres, the hypervisor, the underlying network. Under the shared responsibility model, you are responsible for how you configure what you build on top of that: access permissions, storage visibility, encryption settings, and network rules. Most reported cloud breaches trace back to that second half.

faqs.answer: Overly permissive access — either identity and access management (IAM) roles with far more permission than a user or service actually needs, or storage (like an object storage bucket) left more publicly visible than intended. faqs.answer: Often more, in relative terms. Enterprises typically have a dedicated cloud security or DevOps team reviewing configuration. Many small businesses provision cloud services with default settings and never revisit them, which is precisely the pattern behind most misconfiguration-driven breaches.

title: Cybersecurity Compliance for GCC Businesses: What SAMA and NESA Actually Require
description: Saudi Arabia's SAMA framework and the UAE's NESA regulation set real, specific cybersecurity requirements for regulated businesses. Here is what they actually ask for, in plain language.
bodyMarkdown:
For businesses operating in the Gulf, "cybersecurity compliance" often gets treated as a vague, generic obligation. In practice, the two most significant frameworks in the region — Saudi Arabia's SAMA Cyber Security Framework and the UAE's NESA regulation — have specific, documented technical and governance requirements. Understanding what they actually ask for is more useful than a generic compliance checklist.

## Saudi Arabia: the SAMA Cyber Security Framework

The **Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA)** issued its Cyber Security Framework to give regulated financial institutions — banks, insurance and reinsurance companies — a standardised set of protocols, practices, and methodologies for building cyber resilience. Key elements include:

- **Digital certificate deployment** mandated for critical banking transactions, client authentication, and inter-bank settlement processes.
- **Tiered obligations by organisation size and risk.** Larger, higher-risk institutions face the fullest set of requirements, including mandatory annual self-assessments and SAMA supervisory reviews. Smaller organisations — generally referred to as falling into a scaled or "Class B" category — face a lighter formal audit burden, with independent audits recommended rather than strictly mandated.
- **A consistent baseline regardless of tier**: multi-factor authentication, data encryption, regular backups, and incident logging are treated as minimum requirements across both tiers, not just the larger institutions.

Importantly, insurance and reinsurance companies regulated by SAMA are held to the same mandatory obligations as banks in several respects — this isn't a framework that only concerns traditional banking.

## UAE: the NESA framework

The UAE's **National Electronic Security Authority (NESA)** framework establishes cybersecurity requirements specifically for organisations classified as **critical infrastructure** — a category that in practice extends into financial services, alongside sectors like energy, telecommunications, and government services. NESA's requirements focus on governance, risk management, continuous monitoring, and incident response, with some genuinely specific technical requirements worth knowing:

- **AES-256 encryption required for data at rest.**
- **TLS 1.2 as the minimum standard for data in transit.**
- A structured approach to continuous monitoring rather than point-in-time assessment alone.

## Why this matters even if you're not directly regulated

Most SMEs in the region aren't directly bound by SAMA or NESA — those frameworks apply specifically to regulated financial institutions and critical infrastructure. But the practical reality for a lot of Gulf businesses is that clients, partners, or the banks they work with increasingly _ask_ about alignment with these frameworks, even informally, because they've become the recognisable regional reference point for "is this business handling data responsibly." A business that can point to AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2 minimum in transit, MFA everywhere, and a real incident logging process is answering that question convincingly — regardless of whether a regulator requires it.

## Cross-jurisdictional operations

If your organisation operates in both Saudi Arabia and the UAE and falls within scope of both frameworks — a regulated financial entity with a presence in each market is the clearest example — compliance generally needs to be demonstrated to each regulator independently. The two frameworks share a similar spirit (strong authentication, encryption, monitoring, incident response) but are administered separately, with their own specific documentation and assessment expectations.

## Security recommendations

- **Confirm whether your organisation is actually in scope** for SAMA (financial institutions) or NESA (critical infrastructure) before assuming either applies — and if neither applies directly, treat their baseline controls as a credible reference point rather than an obligation.
- **Implement the shared baseline regardless of formal scope**: MFA across all access points, encryption at rest and in transit meeting or exceeding the AES-256/TLS 1.2 standards NESA specifies, regular tested backups, and real incident logging.
- **Don't wait for a mandatory audit to find gaps.** SAMA's own framework recommends independent audits for smaller institutions even where they aren't compulsory — an independent gap analysis is a low-cost way to know where you actually stand.
- **Document your controls**, not just implement them. Both frameworks emphasise governance and evidence, not just technical configuration — being able to show what you do, and when, matters as much as doing it.
- **Get region-specific compliance guidance before assuming a Western framework (ISO 27001, SOC 2) automatically satisfies a Gulf regulator.** There's meaningful overlap, but SAMA and NESA have their own specific documented requirements that a generic international certification doesn't automatically cover.

## Key takeaways

SAMA and NESA aren't abstract regulatory language — they specify concrete controls (MFA, AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2 in transit, tiered audit obligations, incident logging) that apply directly to regulated financial institutions and critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the UAE respectively, and serve as a credible reference baseline for everyone else in the region. Knowing which framework actually applies to your organisation — and what its baseline controls specifically require — is a more useful starting point than treating "GCC compliance" as one generic obligation.

Shahid Security's [Compliance & Risk Assessment](/services/compliance-risk-assessment/) service maps your current controls against the specific framework you need — including regional and international standards — and builds a realistic remediation plan, not just a checklist.

**Not sure where your business actually stands against the framework that applies to you?** [Book a free consultation](/book/) to talk through a gap analysis.

faqs.answer: No. SAMA's Cyber Security Framework specifically applies to entities regulated by the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority — banks, insurance and reinsurance companies, and similar financial institutions. NESA applies to organisations classified as critical infrastructure in the UAE. Many SMEs outside these categories are not directly bound by either, but often adopt similar controls because clients or partners ask about them.

faqs.answer: SAMA's framework distinguishes tiers of obligation, with smaller organisations generally falling into a scaled category where independent audits are recommended rather than strictly mandatory. Baseline controls — multi-factor authentication, data encryption, regular backups, and incident logging — are treated as a minimum expectation regardless of size.

faqs.answer: If your organisation falls within scope of both — for example, a regulated financial entity with operations in both markets — you may need to demonstrate compliance with each framework independently, since they are administered by different regulators with their own specific requirements.

title: IoT Security in 2026: NIST's Updated Guidance for Connected Devices
description: NIST is updating its core IoT device cybersecurity guidance in 2026, and the EU is imposing new reporting obligations from September 2026. Here is what that means for anyone deploying connected devices.
bodyMarkdown:
Connected devices — cameras, sensors, access control systems, building automation — have quietly become one of the largest and least-monitored parts of most organisations' networks. Two regulatory developments in 2026 are pushing IoT security back onto the agenda: an update to NIST's core device guidance, and new EU reporting obligations that start affecting the market this month.

## NIST's guidance update

NIST has opened a revised draft of its IoT Product Cybersecurity Guidance — **[SP 800-213 Revision 1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-213.pdf)** — for public review, with comments accepted through August 24, 2026. The update strengthens risk management expectations for connected devices used in federal environments, and its core requirements are a genuinely useful checklist for any organisation deploying IoT devices, not just government agencies:

- **Secure coding and vulnerability testing** during development, not bolted on afterward.
- **Secure mechanisms for software and firmware updates** — a device that can't be patched safely and reliably is a liability from day one, regardless of how it was built.
- **Appropriate encryption and integrity verification** to protect data confidentiality and integrity in transit and at rest.
- **Logging, audit, and event monitoring support**, so that a compromise can actually be detected rather than persisting silently — a capability many consumer-grade and even some commercial IoT devices still lack entirely.

## Why this matters right now: scale and the EU deadline

The scale of the underlying problem is significant. Over **21,500 CVEs were disclosed in the first half of 2026 alone** across the software and hardware landscape, and IoT firmware is a disproportionately large and under-patched share of that. Compromised cameras and routers were behind some of the largest recorded DDoS attacks of the past two years, with volumes approaching **30 Tbps** — driven largely by devices running outdated firmware with no realistic update path.

On the regulatory side, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act introduces mandatory reporting obligations for products with digital elements sold in the EU market, with those reporting obligations taking effect **September 11, 2026** — this month — and the fuller set of compliance obligations following in December 2027. Any business selling, integrating, or deploying connected devices with EU market exposure has a genuinely near-term deadline to understand.

## What this looks like in practice: a real example

This isn't abstract for us. Shahid Security's founder's own independent research — [Threats & Attacks on an IoT-Based Smart Campus System](/case-studies/iot-smart-campus-threat-analysis/) — modelled exactly this problem in a controlled academic environment: a smart campus network connecting parking, library access, ID cards, attendance, and exam systems onto shared infrastructure. The research demonstrated a full attack chain — ARP spoofing, traffic interception, DNS spoofing, and downstream script injection — starting from a single compromised device and pivoting into the wider network segment. The root cause wasn't a flaw in any individual sensor or the cloud backend; it was **unauthenticated ARP and DNS resolution** at the network layer, the same category of foundational weakness NIST's guidance is aimed at preventing.

That finding generalises well beyond a university campus: any environment mixing IoT devices with sensitive systems on a flat network — a medical facility, an office building's access control, a retail chain's point-of-sale sensors — carries the same structural risk if devices aren't authenticated and segmented properly.

## Security recommendations

- **Segment IoT devices onto their own network**, separate from the systems holding sensitive data, so a single compromised device isn't a direct path into everything else.
- **Confirm a realistic firmware update path exists before deploying a device**, not after. A device that can't be patched is accumulating risk from the day it's installed.
- **Enable device-level logging where it's supported**, and make sure something actually reviews it — visibility without monitoring provides no real protection.
- **Check for basic network-layer authentication** (address resolution and DNS integrity, not just device passwords) — this was the actual root cause in our own IoT research, not the devices themselves.
- **If you sell or integrate connected products into the EU market, review the Cyber Resilience Act's reporting requirements now**, given the September 2026 obligations are already in effect.

## Key takeaways

IoT security in 2026 is being pushed forward by two forces at once: an updated NIST framework raising the bar on what "secure by design" actually requires, and EU regulation imposing real reporting deadlines starting this month. Underneath both is a consistent technical reality, one we've demonstrated directly in our own independent research: the weakest point in a connected-device environment is often not the device itself, but the unauthenticated network layer it sits on.

Shahid Security's [Penetration Testing](/services/penetration-testing/) service includes IoT and network security assessment, built on hands-on research into exactly this kind of attack chain — not a generic device checklist.

**Deploying or managing connected devices and unsure how exposed the network underneath them really is?** [Book a free consultation](/book/) to talk through an assessment.

faqs.question: What is NIST SP 800-213, and does it apply outside the US government?
faqs.answer: NIST SP 800-213 is federal guidance on IoT device cybersecurity, technically written for US government agencies and their suppliers. In practice, it is widely used as a reference baseline by manufacturers and integrators everywhere, because it is one of the most detailed, freely available frameworks for what "reasonably secure" looks like for a connected device.

faqs.answer: The Cyber Resilience Act introduces mandatory cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements sold in the EU, including vulnerability reporting obligations. Reporting obligations take effect from September 11, 2026, with the main compliance obligations following in December 2027.

faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the most common false assumptions in IoT security. A single compromised device on an internal network can be used to pivot into other systems on the same network segment, which is exactly the attack chain demonstrated in independent IoT research, including our own case study on a smart campus environment.

title: OWASP Top 10:2025 Explained: What Changed and Why It Matters
description: OWASP released its first Top 10 update since 2021 in November 2025. Here is what actually changed, in plain English, and what it means for your next security review.
bodyMarkdown:
Every few years, OWASP updates the Top 10 — its reference list of the most common weaknesses found in web applications — based on data contributed by testing firms and tooling vendors, plus a practitioner survey. The 2025 edition, released in November 2025 at the OWASP Global AppSec conference in Washington, D.C., is the first update since 2021. If your last security review, developer training, or procurement checklist was built around the 2021 list, it's worth understanding what actually moved and why.

This isn't a rewrite of the list itself — OWASP publishes that at [owasp.org/Top10](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/). It's a plain-English walkthrough of what changed, aimed at the people who have to act on it: engineering leads, business owners who commission security reviews, and anyone comparing a report against "the OWASP Top 10" for the first time since 2021.

## The headline change: two new categories

Two categories are genuinely new in 2025, not just renamed:

**A03: Software Supply Chain Failures.** The 2021 list had "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" — essentially, are you running software with known bugs. The 2025 version expands this into something broader: the integrity of how software gets _built and delivered_ in the first place. That includes compromised build pipelines, poisoned open-source packages, and unverified third-party dependencies — not just outdated version numbers. This shift tracks real incidents: 2026 alone saw a widely-used npm package compromised through a maintainer account takeover, distributed to well over a hundred million weekly downloads before anyone caught it (more on that in our [supply chain attacks article](/blog/software-supply-chain-attacks-2026/)).

**A10: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.** This category covers what happens when an application encounters an error, a timeout, or an unexpected input — and handles it badly. That might mean failing open instead of closed, leaking a stack trace with internal details, or silently continuing after a security check throws an exception. It spans 24 different underlying weakness types (CWEs), and it reflects a pattern OWASP's data showed clearly: a lot of real breaches don't come from an attacker breaking strong logic, they come from an attacker triggering the _edge case_ nobody tested.

## What moved, and what that tells you

Beyond the two new entries, the reordering is itself informative:

- **Broken Access Control stays at #1.** It was the most common weakness in 2021 and remains so in 2025 — affecting, per OWASP's data, virtually every application category tested. If your last review didn't dig into authorization logic specifically (not just "is there a login page"), this is the one to revisit first.
- **Security Misconfiguration jumped from #5 to #2.** This is arguably the most practically important move for teams shipping frequently. It signals that the shift to continuous deployment — pushing changes constantly without matching continuous _scanning_ — is creating exposure windows that weren't as common in 2021's slower release cycles.
- **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) was folded into Broken Access Control.** It's not gone; OWASP judged that SSRF is, at its core, an access control failure — the application is making a request it shouldn't be trusted to make — so it made more sense as a symptom of A01 than its own category.
- **The overall framing shifted from symptoms to root causes.** OWASP was explicit about this in the 2025 release notes: rather than cataloguing surface-level bug types, the list increasingly groups issues by the underlying failure in design or process that produced them.

## Why this matters if you're not a developer

If you run a business rather than write code, here's the practical takeaway: the OWASP Top 10 isn't a developer-only reference. It's the de facto standard that penetration testers, auditors, and increasingly cyber-insurance underwriters use to scope and describe what they tested. When a report says "tested against the OWASP Top 10," it's worth knowing whether that means the 2021 or 2025 version — because the 2025 version explicitly asks a tester to look at your build pipeline and third-party dependencies, which a 2021-era scope might have skipped entirely.

This is also a genuinely good moment to ask a question a lot of businesses never ask their developer or agency: _what happens when this app hits an error it wasn't built to expect?_ That's now a named, top-10 category — not an afterthought.

## Security recommendations

- Ask your current or prospective penetration testing provider explicitly which OWASP Top 10 version they scope against, and confirm A03 (supply chain) and A10 (exceptional conditions) are included.
- Inventory your third-party dependencies and packages — not just for known CVEs, but for how they're sourced (official registries with maintainer verification, versus unpinned or loosely-vetted sources).
- Review error-handling paths in your application: what does a user see, and what does the system _do_, when something fails unexpectedly? Fail closed, not open.
- Re-audit access control logic specifically, since it remains the single most common weakness across both the 2021 and 2025 data sets.
- Treat security misconfiguration as a continuous-deployment problem: if you ship weekly, you need scanning on a matching cadence, not an annual review.

## Key takeaways

OWASP's 2025 update is the first in four years, and it reflects real shifts in how applications actually break: supply chain integrity and error-handling behaviour are now named, top-level risk categories rather than footnotes. Broken Access Control remains the most common weakness by a wide margin. If your last security review predates November 2025, it's worth a conversation about whether its scope still matches how attackers are actually getting in.

Shahid Security's [penetration testing](/services/penetration-testing/) engagements are scoped against the current OWASP methodology, including dependency and supply-chain review, not a static checklist from years ago.

**Want a review that reflects the current threat landscape, not last decade's?** [Book a free 30-minute consultation](/book/) to talk through your scope.

---

Sources: [OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/), [OWASP Top 10:2025 Introduction](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/0x00_2025-Introduction/).

faqs.answer: Yes. OWASP released the 2025 edition at its Global AppSec Conference in November 2025, and it supersedes the 2021 list as the current reference. Older audits and checklists built against the 2021 version should be revisited, since two categories are new and several others were reordered or merged.

faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The ranking reflects how frequently OWASP's data sources found each weakness across tested applications, not how severe a single instance can be. A rare but catastrophic issue can rank below a common but usually low-impact one.

faqs.answer: Not automatically. A competent test already covered access control, authentication, misconfiguration and injection regardless of which numbered list they sat under. It is worth asking your tester whether supply-chain integrity and error-handling behaviour — the two genuinely new areas — were in scope, since those are the parts a pre-2025 methodology might have under-covered.

title: A Business Owner's Guide to Patch Management and the CISA KEV Catalog
description: Most businesses cannot patch everything, all the time. Here is how to use CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog to decide what actually needs fixing first.
bodyMarkdown:
Most small and mid-sized businesses have the same patching problem: dozens of systems, a handful of people who can actually apply updates, and a constant stream of vendor advisories saying everything is "critical." Patching everything immediately isn't realistic. Patching nothing until something breaks isn't safe either. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) publishes a free, public tool that solves exactly this prioritisation problem — and most businesses outside the US federal government have never heard of it.

## What the KEV catalog actually is

CISA's [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) is a running list of specific software vulnerabilities that CISA has confirmed are being actively exploited by attackers — right now, in the real world, not in a lab. This is a meaningfully different signal from a general vendor security bulletin. A vendor's "critical" rating usually reflects how bad a vulnerability _could_ be if exploited. The KEV catalog only lists vulnerabilities that already _are_ being exploited, based on threat intelligence CISA has verified.

The catalog moves constantly. In the first three weeks of September 2026 alone, CISA added vulnerabilities affecting Sangoma Switchvox, Adobe Commerce/Magento, Microsoft Windows, Fortinet products, Citrix NetScaler, Cisco Firewall Management Center and Identity Services Engine, N-able N-central, Acronis Backup, and Zyxel switches — a genuinely broad spread of vendors, which is normal for the catalog. It isn't specific to one platform or industry.

CISA pairs the catalog with **Binding Operational Directive 26-04**, which sets mandatory remediation deadlines for US federal agencies once a vulnerability is added. Your business isn't bound by that directive — but the underlying signal (this is confirmed to be exploited, not theoretical) is exactly as useful to a private business as it is to a federal agency.

## Why this beats a generic "patch everything" policy

A patch management policy that treats every update as equally urgent tends to produce one of two failure modes: either nothing gets patched on schedule because the backlog is overwhelming, or patches get applied in a rush without testing, which occasionally breaks something in production. Using the KEV catalog as a prioritisation layer avoids both:

1. **Confirmed exploitation beats theoretical severity.** A vulnerability with a lower severity score that's on the KEV list is a more urgent real-world risk than a higher-scored vulnerability with no known exploitation. Attackers go after what's already proven to work.
2. **It's vendor-neutral.** You don't need a subscription to every vendor's threat feed. CISA's list already aggregates across vendors.
3. **It tells you what to do next, not just what's wrong.** Most KEV entries link to the vendor's official advisory and a remediation deadline, which is a ready-made action item rather than another thing to research.

## A practical patch prioritisation approach for SMEs

You don't need a dedicated security team to use this. A workable process looks like:

- **Know what you're running.** You can't prioritise patches for software you don't know you have. A basic asset inventory — servers, key business applications, network devices, cloud services — is the prerequisite for everything else.
- **Check new assets and major software against the KEV catalog on a regular cadence** (weekly is reasonable for most SMEs), not just when a vendor sends an alert.
- **Prioritise internet-facing systems first.** A KEV-listed vulnerability on a public web server or VPN gateway is a materially higher near-term risk than the same vulnerability on an internal-only machine with no direct internet exposure.
- **Set a real deadline once something matches**, and treat it the way CISA's own federal directive does: days, not "whenever we get to it."
- **Don't stop patching everything else.** The KEV catalog tells you what's urgent, not what's optional. Routine patching on a monthly cycle still matters for the vulnerabilities that haven't been weaponised yet.

## Security recommendations

- Bookmark the [CISA KEV catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) and check it against your software inventory on a set schedule.
- Maintain a current, honest asset inventory — this is the single most common gap we see, and it undermines every other step.
- Segment and prioritise internet-facing systems for the fastest patch cycle.
- Where a full internal patch program isn't realistic, a periodic external vulnerability assessment closes the gap by checking what's actually exposed from outside.

## Key takeaways

Patch management doesn't have to mean patching everything immediately — it means patching the right things first. CISA's KEV catalog is a free, continuously updated, vendor-neutral signal built specifically to answer "what's actually being exploited right now," and it's available to any business, not just US federal agencies. Combined with a basic asset inventory and a bias toward internet-facing systems, it turns an overwhelming backlog into a manageable, evidence-based priority list.

Shahid Security's [Vulnerability Assessment & Security Audit](/services/vulnerability-assessment/) service maps your actual attack surface and cross-checks it against known-exploited and misconfigured issues, so you have a prioritised, realistic fix list rather than a wall of "critical" alerts.

**Not sure what's actually exposed on your network right now?** [Book a free consultation](/book/) and we'll help you find out.

faqs.answer: The mandatory remediation deadlines apply to US federal agencies, but the catalog itself is public and free for anyone to use. Because it only lists vulnerabilities with confirmed real-world exploitation, it is one of the most reliable free signals any business can use to prioritise patching.

title: Ransomware in 2026: Why Attacks Are Faster and Harder to Detect
description: Modern ransomware groups move from initial access to full compromise in minutes, not days, and increasingly avoid malware altogether. Here is what changed and what actually helps.
bodyMarkdown:
Ransomware headlines tend to focus on the ransom amount or the company name. The more operationally important story in 2026 is about speed and stealth: how fast attackers move once they're in, and how much of that movement is designed to look completely normal until it's too late.

## The numbers, from CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report

CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report gives some of the clearest current data on how ransomware and broader eCrime operations actually behave:

- **Average breakout time — the time from initial access to broader lateral movement — dropped to roughly 29 minutes.** The fastest recorded instance was just **27 seconds**.
- **82% of detections in 2025 were "malware-free."** Rather than deploying obviously malicious software that antivirus tools are built to catch, attackers increasingly use legitimate administrative tools and valid, often stolen, credentials already present in the environment.
- **AI-enabled attacks rose 89%** year over year, reflecting broader adoption of AI tooling by attackers — from automating credential theft to nation-state actors deploying LLM-powered malware.
- **Cloud-conscious intrusions — attacks specifically designed around cloud environments — rose 37% overall, and 266% among state-nexus (nation-state-linked) actors.** Ransomware groups are increasingly comfortable operating across cloud, identity, and virtualization layers, not just traditional on-premise networks.
- **Supply chain compromise was a defining tactic of 2025**, with adversaries targeting upstream software providers and public code repositories to gain broad, indirect access to many downstream organisations at once (see our related article on [software supply chain attacks](/blog/software-supply-chain-attacks-2026/)).

## Two emerging shifts worth knowing about specifically

**Encryptionless extortion.** As ransom payment rates have declined — more organisations either refuse to pay or have recovery capability that removes the pressure to pay — some groups have shifted tactics entirely. Rather than encrypting data and demanding payment for the decryption key, they steal the data and threaten to leak it, skipping encryption altogether. The business impact (extortion, reputational risk, regulatory exposure) remains, even though the technical signature looks different from classic ransomware.

**Post-quantum cryptography in new ransomware families.** Some newly observed ransomware strains have begun adopting post-quantum-resistant encryption ciphers — a forward-looking move by attackers that has no near-term practical effect on victims today, but signals that ransomware tooling is being actively developed and hardened, not stagnating.

## Why "malware-free" and "fast" together are the real problem

The combination of these two trends is what makes modern ransomware genuinely harder to defend against than the ransomware of a few years ago. A malware-free intrusion using legitimate tools and valid credentials doesn't trigger the same alarms a piece of custom malware would. Combined with a breakout time measured in minutes, the practical window for a human security analyst to notice something's wrong, investigate, and contain it before it spreads has compressed dramatically. This isn't a reason for panic — it's a reason to make sure detection and response capability, not just prevention, is part of your security posture.

## Security recommendations

- **Assume prevention will occasionally fail, and invest in detection accordingly.** Monitoring for unusual use of legitimate admin tools (not just malware signatures) is now a baseline requirement, not an advanced capability.
- **Maintain and actually test backups on a 3-2-1 basis** (three copies, two different media, one off-site or offline) — the single factor that most changes your options during an active incident.
- **Segment identity and cloud access** so that a compromised credential in one system doesn't provide a fast path to everything else, especially given the sharp rise in cloud-conscious intrusions.
- **Have an incident response plan written down before you need it.** Deciding roles, communication steps, and escalation paths during an active incident costs time you don't have; deciding them in advance is free.
- **Review third-party and supply chain access regularly** given how often 2025's major incidents traced back to a trusted upstream provider rather than a direct attack.

## Key takeaways

The defining shift in ransomware behaviour in 2026 isn't a new kind of malware — it's speed and camouflage. Breakout times measured in minutes, combined with attackers increasingly using legitimate tools and credentials rather than obvious malware, mean that detection and tested recovery capability matter as much as prevention. Businesses with a tested backup strategy and a written incident response plan aren't just recovering faster when something happens; they're negotiating from a position where paying a ransom is a choice, not a necessity.

faqs.question: What does "breakout time" mean, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Breakout time is how long it takes an attacker to move from their initial foothold on one machine to broader access across your network. As that window shrinks, the time your team has to detect and contain an intrusion before it becomes a full-blown incident shrinks with it.

faqs.question: If most attacks are now "malware-free," how are they still dangerous?
faqs.answer: Malware-free means the attacker is using legitimate tools and valid credentials already present in your environment, rather than installing obviously malicious software. This makes the activity much harder for traditional antivirus-style detection to catch, because nothing looks like malware — it looks like a normal admin doing normal admin tasks, until it isn't.

faqs.question: Is paying a ransom ever the right call?

title: Software Supply Chain Attacks: Lessons from the 2026 npm Compromises
description: A widely-used npm package with over 100 million weekly downloads was hijacked in 2026 through a single compromised maintainer account. Here is what happened and what it means for any business relying on open-source software.
bodyMarkdown:
On March 31, 2026, Axios — a widely used npm package for making HTTP requests in JavaScript applications, with over 100 million weekly downloads — was compromised. It's one of a growing number of 2026 incidents that illustrate a specific and uncomfortable reality: your application's security depends on the security practices of maintainers you've never met, working on projects you may not even know you depend on.

## What happened

According to security researchers and CISA's own advisory, the Axios compromise wasn't caused by a flaw in the package's code. It was an **account takeover** — attackers gained control of a lead maintainer's npm publishing account, reportedly changing its associated email to lock out the legitimate owner, and bypassed the project's GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline protections to publish a malicious version. CISA published an advisory on the incident on **April 20, 2026**, and the compromise has been attributed to a North Korean threat actor.

This wasn't an isolated case. March 2026 alone saw five major software supply chain attacks, including compromises affecting **Trivy** (a widely used vulnerability scanner), **KICS** (a static analysis tool), **LiteLLM** (an interface for AI models), and **Telnyx** (a real-time communications library) — attributed to a group tracked as TeamPCP. Later in the year, a separate campaign known as **ChainDrop** spread through hundreds of npm packages in August 2026, specifically targeting developer and cloud credentials.

## The Shai-Hulud shift: from nuisance to self-propagating

Perhaps the most structurally important development in this space is what security researchers have called the **Shai-Hulud worm** — a self-replicating malware pattern that automates the compromise and redistribution of malicious npm packages. Earlier generations of supply chain attacks were largely manual: an attacker compromises one package, and the damage is limited to what that package touches. A self-propagating worm changes the economics entirely — one successful compromise can automatically spread to other packages the same maintainer or infrastructure touches, without further attacker effort. Industry researchers have described this as marking the end of the "nuisance" era of npm attacks and the start of a genuinely high-consequence one.

## Why package managers alone don't protect you

It's worth being direct about a common misconception: using a reputable package manager doesn't mean the packages you install are vetted the way, say, a mobile app store review process might vet an app. npm, PyPI, and similar registries are largely open publishing platforms — anyone with a maintainer account can push a new version, and that version becomes immediately available to every downstream project with a matching or unpinned version range. The registry infrastructure itself wasn't what failed in the Axios case; a single human account was.

## Security recommendations

- **Pin dependency versions rather than using open ranges**, so a compromised new release doesn't get pulled into your build automatically the next time you install or update.
- **Review your dependency tree periodically, including transitive (indirect) dependencies** — the packages your packages depend on, which is where a lot of real exposure hides unnoticed.
- **Use lockfiles and verify them in CI**, so an unexpected change to a dependency's resolved version is visible in a code review rather than silent.
- **Monitor official advisories** — CISA, GitHub's security advisories, and package-specific security mailing lists — for the specific packages your application actually depends on.
- **Apply least-privilege to your own CI/CD pipeline and publishing credentials** if you maintain packages yourself, including hardware-backed or short-lived tokens rather than long-lived static credentials, which is exactly the kind of control that would have blunted the Axios account-takeover pattern.
- **Include supply chain review in code review and pre-launch security testing**, not just a one-time dependency audit — this is precisely the gap OWASP's new [Software Supply Chain Failures category](/blog/owasp-top-10-2025-explained/) in the 2025 Top 10 was introduced to address.

## Key takeaways

The Axios compromise and the broader wave of 2026 npm attacks share a common lesson: modern software supply chain risk is often a human and process failure — a compromised maintainer account, a bypassed CI/CD safeguard — rather than a technical flaw in the code itself. With self-propagating patterns like Shai-Hulud emerging, the practical response for any business building software isn't to avoid open-source dependencies (that's not realistic), but to pin versions, monitor advisories, and build supply chain review into how software actually gets shipped.

faqs.question: If we do not publish open-source packages ourselves, are we still at risk from these attacks?
faqs.answer: Yes. The risk applies to anyone who consumes open-source packages, which in practice means almost every modern software project. A compromised package you depend on — even indirectly, several layers deep in your dependency tree — can affect your application without you ever having published anything yourself.

faqs.question: How was a package with 100 million weekly downloads compromised so easily?
faqs.answer: Reported analysis attributes the compromise to an account takeover targeting a lead maintainer, rather than a flaw in the package's own code. Attackers bypassed the project's CI/CD pipeline protections by compromising the maintainer's npm account and changing its associated email — a human and process weakness, not a code vulnerability.

faqs.question: What is the Shai-Hulud worm mentioned in supply chain security coverage?
faqs.answer: It is a self-replicating malware pattern observed in 2025 that automated the compromise and redistribution of malicious npm packages, marking a shift from isolated, manually-executed supply chain attacks toward automated, self-propagating ones — a meaningfully more dangerous category.
